briefing.title: Rome, AD 41
paragraphs: January AD 41. The emperor has just been murdered by officers of his own bodyguard, and the killers seem ready to wipe out his whole family. Behind a palace curtain cowers his uncle Claudius, a limping, stammering scholar whom everyone has dismissed as a fool.

What follows is 27 years of two very different emperors: Claudius, who conquers Britain and runs the empire with surprising skill, and his stepson Nero, a singing artist-emperor whose reign brings fire, revolt and finally civil war. Can any ruler survive Rome's Senate, soldiers and family?

timelines.name: Two Emperors
timelines.blurb: The big turning points from Claudius's birth to Nero's death.

events.label: Claudius born at Lugdunum
events.fact: Born at Lugdunum, modern Lyon, Claudius was the first Roman emperor born outside Italy.

events.label: Four legions invade Britain
events.fact: Claudius sent four legions across the Channel after a British ally driven from his lands appealed for help.

events.label: Great Fire breaks out in Rome
events.fact: Starting near the Circus Maximus, the fire destroyed three of Rome's fourteen districts and badly damaged seven more.

events.label: Nero dies outside Rome
events.fact: Abandoned by his guards and declared a public enemy, Nero stabbed himself at a freedman's villa, and his dynasty died with him.

timelines.name: Power and Family
timelines.blurb: Offices, heirs and murders across two reigns.

events.label: Claudius serves as consul
events.fact: Claudius finally held a top office alongside his nephew, the reigning emperor, who mocked and humiliated him.

events.label: Claudius hailed emperor
events.fact: After his nephew's murder, tradition says a guardsman found Claudius behind a curtain and hailed him as emperor.

events.label: Claudius revives the censorship
events.fact: As censor, keeper of the lists of citizens and senators, Claudius admitted nobles from Gaul into the Senate.

events.label: Claudius adopts Agrippina's son
events.fact: Claudius renamed the boy Nero, married him to his daughter and made him joint heir with Britannicus.

events.label: Nero has his mother killed
events.fact: Ancient writers say a freedman arranged a shipwreck, then murdered Agrippina when she swam ashore and called it suicide.

events.label: Nero competes at the Olympic Games
events.fact: Nero won every contest in Greece, even a chariot race in which he fell out and never finished.

timelines.name: Year by Year
timelines.blurb: A tighter sequence of plots, projects and revolts.

events.label: Nero born at Antium
events.fact: Nero was born Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus at Antium, a seaside town south of Rome.

events.label: Claudius's third wife weds her lover
events.fact: While Claudius was away at Ostia, his third wife publicly married a senator; she was executed.

events.label: Two new aqueducts reach Rome
events.fact: Claudius was a great builder, and two new aqueducts brought water into the city.

events.label: Claudius dies, aged 63
events.fact: Nearly all ancient writers blamed Agrippina and poisoned mushrooms, though some modern historians doubt the murder.

events.label: Britannicus is poisoned
events.fact: Claudius's son was poisoned after Agrippina threatened to back him against Nero.

events.label: Boudica leads the Iceni in revolt
events.fact: After Rome seized her late husband's kingdom, Boudica's rebels burned Camulodunum, Londinium and Verulamium.

events.label: Senators' plot against Nero betrayed
events.fact: A conspiracy of senators and guard officers was betrayed, and Nero's old tutor was ordered to kill himself.

events.label: Governor in Gaul rebels against Nero
events.fact: The governor rebelled against Nero's taxes and urged the governor of Spain to claim the throne.

matchSets.name: Places of the Age
matchSets.blurb: Match each place to its role in the story.

pairs.name: Lugdunum
pairs.match: Modern Lyon, where Claudius was born in 10 BC

pairs.name: Camulodunum
pairs.match: Veterans' colony with Claudius's temple, Boudica's first target

pairs.name: Antium
pairs.match: Seaside town where Nero was born and stayed as the fire began

pairs.name: Ostia
pairs.match: Rome's port, near which Claudius built a harbour with a lighthouse

pairs.name: Fucine Lake
pairs.match: Its drainage tunnel flooded a gladiator show

matchSets.name: Words of Power
matchSets.blurb: Match each Roman term to its meaning.

pairs.name: Praetorian Guard
pairs.match: Elite bodyguard in Rome that made Claudius emperor

pairs.name: Censor
pairs.match: Revived office that kept the lists of citizens and senators

pairs.name: Freedmen
pairs.match: Former slaves who headed Claudius's offices for letters and finance

pairs.name: Golden House
pairs.match: Nero's new palace with parks and a 30 m statue of himself

pairs.name: Damnatio memoriae
pairs.match: Condemnation of a ruler's memory; Nero's portraits were defaced

trueFalseDecks.name: Claudius
trueFalseDecks.blurb: The scholar who became emperor by accident.

cards.claim: Claudius wrote twenty books on Carthage.
cards.why: His twenty books were on the Etruscans, who ruled much of Italy before Rome; he wrote eight on Carthage.

cards.claim: Claudius rewarded each guardsman with 15,000 sesterces.
cards.why: Critics called it the first time an emperor bought the army's loyalty, though earlier emperors had left similar gifts in their wills.

cards.claim: Claudius went before the Senate to win its approval before taking power.
cards.why: The Senate demanded he appear, but he wisely refused, and the senators were forced to accept him.

cards.claim: Claudius's census of AD 48 counted about a million fewer citizens than a generation before.
cards.why: It counted 5,984,072 adult male citizens, about a million more than a generation before.

cards.claim: Claudius ruled that sick slaves abandoned on an island in the Tiber were free if they recovered.
cards.why: Claudius loved law and judged many cases himself; this was one of his famous rulings.

cards.claim: Claudius spent just sixteen days in Britain.
cards.why: He crossed over with reinforcements once the first fighting was over and stayed only sixteen days.

cards.claim: Claudius proudly took the title "Britannicus" for himself.
cards.why: He took the title only for his baby son, who became known as Britannicus.

cards.claim: Claudius died on 13 October AD 54, aged 63.
cards.why: Ancient writers blamed Agrippina for poisoning him, but some modern historians doubt the murder.

trueFalseDecks.name: Nero
trueFalseDecks.blurb: Artist, emperor and the villain of the sources.

cards.claim: Nero became emperor at the age of 16.
cards.why: When Claudius died in AD 54, the Praetorian Guard and the Senate backed the 16-year-old.

cards.claim: Tacitus blamed Nero's first wife for the murder of Agrippina.
cards.why: Tacitus blamed Nero's mistress; modern historians doubt this, since Nero married her only three years later.

cards.claim: Boudica's husband left his kingdom jointly to their two daughters and Nero.
cards.why: When he died, Rome ignored his will and seized the kingdom, sparking the revolt.

cards.claim: The Roman governor crushed Boudica with about 100,000 men.
cards.why: He had almost 10,000 men and was heavily outnumbered, but won with javelins and a wedge charge.

cards.claim: The Great Fire destroyed ten of Rome's fourteen districts outright.
cards.why: Three districts were destroyed and seven more badly damaged.

cards.claim: According to Tacitus, Nero blamed the Christians for the fire.
cards.why: Many Christians were thrown to wild beasts, crucified or burned alive, out of cruelty rather than justice.

cards.claim: Nero died at a freedman's villa about 6 km (four miles) outside Rome.
cards.why: He fled there in disguise and stabbed himself in the throat with his secretary's help as horsemen approached.

cards.claim: Tacitus and the other main writers on Nero wrote within ten years of his death.
cards.why: Tacitus and the biographer wrote more than fifty years after Nero's death, the Greek senator more than 150.

oddOneOut.why: Boudica's rebels attacked and burned Camulodunum, Londinium and Verulamium; Anglesey is the island in Wales where the governor was campaigning.
Claudius wrote books on the Etruscans, Carthage and dice; the fall of Troy is what Nero was said to sing about while Rome burned.
The aqueducts, harbour and tunnel were Claudius's projects; the Golden House was Nero's palace built after the fire.

items: His food taster kept his job
Nero wed his mistress years later
oddOneOut.why: The first three are why some modern historians doubt Claudius was murdered; the late marriage is why they doubt Nero's mistress drove him to kill Agrippina.

items: Paid to clear bodies and rubble
Opened his palaces to the homeless
oddOneOut.why: Nero cleared rubble, sheltered the homeless and brought food after the fire; insuring merchants on winter voyages to Egypt was Claudius's policy.
The others belong to Nero's promising early years; treason trials returned only after his mother's murder.
Almost everything we know comes from Tacitus, the biographer and the Greek senator; the Jewish historian only complained about flattering and lying writers.

whoAmI.name: The Imperial Family
whoAmI.blurb: Emperors and heirs of a deadly dynasty.

people.name: Claudius
clues: I wrote twenty books on the Etruscans and even one on dice.
My own mother called me a monster and her yardstick for stupidity.
A guardsman found me hiding behind a curtain and hailed me emperor.
I was born at Lugdunum and sent four legions to conquer Britain.

people.name: Nero
clues: I was born at Antium, a seaside town south of Rome, in AD 37.
I won every contest at the Olympic Games, even a race I never finished.
Rumours said I started the Great Fire to make room for my Golden House.
I became emperor at 16 after my stepfather died in AD 54.

people.name: Britannicus
clues: I was still a child when my father married his own niece.
My father had begun talking of my coming of age shortly before he died.
My name comes from a victory title my father refused for himself.
Claudius's own son by birth, I was poisoned in AD 55.

whoAmI.name: Queens and Chroniclers
whoAmI.blurb: A rebel queen, an empress and the historian who told their stories.

people.name: Boudica
clues: Later centuries made me a national heroine.
My husband left his kingdom jointly to our two daughters and the emperor.
My rebels burned Londinium and Verulamium.
I was queen of the Iceni, a tribe in what is now Norfolk.

people.name: Agrippina
clues: My portrait appeared on my son's coins in the place reserved for the emperor.
A great-granddaughter of the first emperor, I married my own uncle.
Ancient writers said I poisoned my husband with mushrooms.
My son had me killed in AD 59 after a staged shipwreck.

people.name: Tacitus
clues: I admitted that histories of these emperors were falsified out of fear while they lived.
I noted that Nero was at Antium when the Great Fire began.
I blamed Nero's mistress for the murder of his mother.
I am the senator-historian whose Annals give the fullest account of Nero.

places.name: Lugdunum
places.why: Claudius was born here, modern Lyon, and a bronze plaque found here preserves his speech admitting Gallic nobles to the Senate.

places.name: Camulodunum
places.why: Capital of the new province of Britain with a great temple to Claudius, it was the first target of Boudica's revolt.

places.name: Anglesey
places.why: The governor was campaigning on this Welsh island when Boudica's revolt broke out.

places.name: Egypt
places.why: Claudius insured merchants who risked winter voyages to Egypt to end Rome's grain shortages.

places.name: Greece
places.why: In AD 67 Nero competed at the Olympic Games in Greece and won every contest.
